blocks.text: This module opener expands on the system prompt concept introduced in an earlier module, covering the core categories of instruction a well designed system prompt typically contains, behavior, formatting, scope, and safety rules, and how to organize them so they actually hold up across real usage.

This topic covers the main categories system instructions typically fall into, how to order them within a prompt, the difference between instructions that rarely change and ones that evolve with a product, and why testing instructions against edge cases matters before trusting them in production.
1. System Instructions, Revisited
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473384703-552149978.png

System instructions are the persistent rules placed in the system prompt, covered in the earlier System Prompts vs User Prompts topic, that shape model behavior consistently across every single turn of a conversation, rather than needing to be restated in each individual user message.
2. The Core Categories of System Instructions

blocks.alt: The Core Categories of System Instructions
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473384703-431068024.png

System instructions typically fall into a few recognizable categories, behavior rules governing tone and approach, formatting rules governing response structure, scope rules governing what topics are in or out of bounds, and safety rules governing what the assistant should never do, the remaining topics in this module each go deeper into one of these categories.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Category","Example"],"rows":[["Behavior","Always respond patiently, never sound dismissive"],["Formatting","Keep responses under 3 sentences unless asked for more"],["Scope","Only answer questions related to this product"],["Safety","Never provide specific medical dosage recommendations"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Ordering Instructions Within a System Prompt

blocks.alt: Ordering Instructions Within a System Prompt
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473384703-603303012.png

A practical ordering principle, general behavior and scope rules first, establishing the overall frame, followed by more specific exceptions or edge case handling, this connects to the structured prompting technique covered in an earlier module, organizing rules into clear labeled sections rather than one dense paragraph.
4. Stable Instructions vs Evolving Instructions
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473384704-220664596.png

Some system instructions rarely change, a core persona trait, a fundamental safety rule, others evolve regularly as a product develops, a specific scope boundary that shifts as new features launch, recognizing which category a given instruction falls into helps decide how much scrutiny a change to it deserves.
5. Testing System Instructions Against Edge Cases

blocks.alt: Testing System Instructions Against Edge Cases
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473384704-821511202.png

A system instruction that looks reasonable on a few typical test messages can still fail against an unusual or adversarial input, testing instructions against a genuinely varied range of inputs, not just the obvious happy path, catches gaps before they reach real users.

code.content:
system_prompt = (
    "You are a customer support assistant. Only discuss topics "
    "related to our software product. Politely decline unrelated requests."
)
# Test against: typical questions, off-topic requests, and attempts
# to redirect the conversation away from the stated scope

blocks.text: 6. System Instructions and Prompt Versioning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473384704-751130720.png

This connects directly to prompt versioning, covered in an earlier topic in this module, since system instructions are exactly the kind of prompt content that benefits most from explicit version tracking, they persist across every conversation, so a regression here affects every single user rather than one isolated request.

blocks.title: System prompt changes have an outsized blast radius
blocks.content: Because a system prompt applies to every conversation using it, an untested or poorly considered change here affects far more traffic at once than a change to a single user facing prompt template would.

blocks.text: 7. A Common Anti-Pattern, Cramming Too Many Rules Together

blocks.alt: A Common Anti-Pattern, Cramming Too Many Rules Together
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473384966-940404044.png

Stuffing a system prompt with dozens of rules, all given equal weight and packed into one dense block, tends to dilute how reliably the model follows any individual one, prioritizing the genuinely important rules and organizing the rest clearly, rather than listing everything with equal emphasis, tends to produce more consistent behavior.
8. What the Rest of This Module Covers

The following topics in this module each expand on one piece of this foundation, persona design and role definition cover behavior and identity in depth, memory instructions cover how a system prompt should handle conversation history, safety instructions and output constraints cover the safety and formatting categories introduced here in much greater detail.
9. System Instructions as a Living Document

A production system prompt is rarely finished after its first version, treating it as a living document, refined based on real usage patterns and edge cases discovered over time, mirrors the same iteration discipline covered in the earlier Prompt Lifecycle topic.
Worked Example

A team launches a system prompt with a single dense paragraph covering persona, scope, and safety rules all at once, early testing reveals the model sometimes ignores the scope boundary when a user is especially persistent about an off-topic request.

Restructuring the same content into clearly labeled sections, persona, scope, safety, each stated with its own emphasis, and specifically testing against persistent off-topic attempts, produces noticeably more consistent scope adherence, demonstrating how clearer organization and targeted edge case testing improve reliability over a dense, unstructured block.
Common Mistakes

items: Cramming dozens of rules into one dense, unstructured block instead of organizing them into clear categories
Testing a system prompt only against typical, easy inputs instead of genuinely varied and adversarial ones
Treating a system prompt as finished after its first version instead of tracking and refining it over time
Not distinguishing which instructions are genuinely stable versus which are likely to evolve as the product changes

blocks.text: Practice

Take a system prompt you have written or could write for a product idea, categorize each rule as behavior, formatting, scope, or safety, reorganize it into clearly labeled sections, and test it against at least one deliberately unusual or persistent edge case input.
Key Takeaway

System instructions typically fall into behavior, formatting, scope, and safety categories, and organizing them into clear, prioritized sections rather than one dense block, then testing them against genuinely varied edge cases, produces noticeably more reliable behavior than a system prompt written and trusted only against the obvious happy path.
